meta.titre: Radio Communication: Modulation, the Receiver, AM and FM, and Cell Phones
meta.sous_theme: Radio communication: signals, receivers and mobile networks

sections.contenu_markdown: In a village near Bafia a farmer listens to the news on a small battery radio, and the same afternoon his daughter's phone loses its signal behind the thick concrete walls of the new market building. Both depend on electromagnetic waves, but they use different frequencies, different ways of carrying the information and different routes through the air. The GCE examiners like short, precise questions on this theme: what a signal is, what VHF and UHF mean, what each part of a radio receiver does, and how AM differs from FM. They also set simple calculations on wavelength and on the tuned circuit.

items: Electromagnetic waves travel at $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air and obey $c=f\lambda$.
The energy of a photon of an electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ is $E=hf$, with $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.
An inductor $L$ and a capacitor $C$ connected together form a circuit that oscillates at one natural frequency, and a diode lets current pass in one direction only.

sections.titre: Signals, modulation, bands and the tuned receiver
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Signals and modulation.** A **signal** is a varying voltage, current or wave that carries information, for example the audio signal from a microphone. Audio frequencies (about $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\ \mathrm{kHz}$) cannot be radiated efficiently, because the aerial would have to be several kilometres long, and all stations would transmit in the same range of frequencies and overlap. So the audio signal is combined with a high-frequency **carrier** wave in a process called **modulation**. In **amplitude modulation (AM)** the amplitude of the carrier varies in step with the signal, while its frequency stays constant. In **frequency modulation (FM)** the frequency of the carrier varies in step with the signal amplitude, while the amplitude stays constant.

**Frequency bands.** VHF means **very high frequency** ($30\ \mathrm{MHz}$ to $300\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and UHF means **ultra high frequency** ($300\ \mathrm{MHz}$ to $3\ \mathrm{GHz}$); HF (high frequency) is $3$ to $30\ \mathrm{MHz}$ and MF (medium frequency) is $300\ \mathrm{kHz}$ to $3\ \mathrm{MHz}$. The wavelength is $\lambda=c/f$. A UHF photon has more energy than a VHF photon because $E=hf$; the power that a transmitter radiates depends on its amplitude and electrical power input.

**Routes of propagation.**

| Wave | Frequencies | How it travels |
|---|---|---|
| Ground (surface) wave | up to about $3\ \mathrm{MHz}$ | follows the curvature of the Earth |
| Sky wave | HF, about $3$ to $30\ \mathrm{MHz}$ | refracted back by the ionosphere, for long distances |
| Space wave | VHF and UHF | direct line of sight between aerials; not bent back by the ionosphere |

Television stations use space waves, so tall mast aerials increase the range and hills or buildings block the signal.

**The radio receiver.** The aerial picks up many stations at once. The **LC loop** (tuned circuit) selects the wanted station: it has maximum response at its resonant frequency
$$f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$
and a variable capacitor changes $C$ to tune to a different station. The **demodulator** (detector) removes the carrier and recovers the audio signal: a diode rectifies the modulated wave and a capacitor smooths it. The audio amplifier then drives the loudspeaker.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks you to compare the two methods in terms of noise, range and bandwidth.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | AM | FM |
|---|---|---|
| Noise interference | Noise and lightning add small changes to the amplitude, so they are heard as noise | Noise mostly changes the amplitude, which the FM receiver ignores, so reception is clearer |
| Broadcast range | Long range on MF and HF because ground and sky waves are used | Shorter range (line of sight, tens of kilometres) because VHF space waves are used |
| Bandwidth | Narrow: $2f_m$ where $f_m$ is the highest audio frequency, so about $10\ \mathrm{kHz}$ per station | Wide: about $200\ \mathrm{kHz}$ per broadcast station |

In AM a carrier $f_c$ modulated by a pure tone $f_m$ contains $f_c-f_m$, $f_c$ and $f_c+f_m$; the two outer frequencies are the sidebands and the bandwidth is $2f_m$. Because FM needs a wide band, it is used at VHF where there is more spectrum. The wide band also allows higher-quality sound, which is why FM is preferred for music.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question concerns a cell site, poor reception near buildings, or the meaning of roaming.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A mobile network divides an area into **cells**, each served by a base station (cell site) with its own aerial. Neighbouring cells use different frequencies and the same frequencies are reused in cells that are far apart. When a user moves from one cell to the next, the call is handed over to the new base station without a break.

Cell phones use UHF space waves, which travel in straight lines and bend little around obstacles. Reception is poor in front of a tall concrete building that backs a cell site for these reasons: (i) the building absorbs and attenuates the signal, and the reinforcing steel reflects it, so the phone is in a **shadow** of the building; (ii) the signal reaching the phone by several paths (direct and reflected) arrives out of phase and partly cancels (multipath interference).

A phone is **roaming** when it is used outside the coverage area of its home network and connects through another operator's network (a visited network) which has an agreement with its own operator.

sections.enonce_markdown: The tuned circuit of an AM radio contains a coil of inductance $200\ \mu\mathrm{H}$ and a variable capacitor. (a) Calculate the capacitance needed to receive a station of frequency $900\ \mathrm{kHz}$. (b) Find the wavelength of the station's carrier wave. (c) By what factor must the capacitance be changed to tune to a station of frequency $1800\ \mathrm{kHz}$?

etapes.justification: The circuit responds most strongly to the station whose frequency equals the natural frequency of the LC circuit.
Squaring both sides removes the square root, and then $C$ can be separated from the other quantities.

etapes.action: Substitute with SI units for part (a).

etapes.justification: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, so they travel at $c$ in air.

etapes.action: Compare the two stations for part (c).
etapes.justification: Since $C\propto1/f_0^2$, doubling the frequency divides the capacitance by $2^2=4$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The capacitor must be set to **156 pF**, the wavelength is **333 m**, and to receive a station at twice the frequency the capacitance must be reduced to **one quarter** of its value (**39.1 pF**).

items.erreur_markdown: Defining a signal as "a wave that travels through the air" or as "a radio wave".
items.pourquoi_faux: A signal is the information, not the wave. The radio wave is only the carrier of it.
items.correction_markdown: A signal is a varying voltage, current or wave that carries information, such as speech or music.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that the demodulator makes the signal stronger, or that the LC loop amplifies the signal.
items.pourquoi_faux: Amplifiers increase the amplitude. The demodulator recovers the audio signal from the modulated carrier, and the LC loop selects one station.
items.correction_markdown: Demodulator (detector): removes the carrier and recovers the audio signal. LC loop (tuned circuit): selects the wanted station by resonance.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that in FM the amplitude of the carrier changes, and that FM has a narrower bandwidth than AM.
items.pourquoi_faux: In FM it is the frequency of the carrier that varies with the signal, and the band needed is wider, about $200\ \mathrm{kHz}$ against about $10\ \mathrm{kHz}$.
items.correction_markdown: AM: amplitude varies, frequency constant, narrow band. FM: frequency varies, amplitude constant, wide band, less noise.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that VHF and UHF waves are reflected by the ionosphere and so reach far countries.
items.pourquoi_faux: Waves of such high frequency pass through the ionosphere. They are space waves and travel in straight lines, so the range is limited by the horizon.
items.correction_markdown: Long-distance ionospheric reflection applies to HF sky waves. VHF and UHF need line of sight, tall masts or satellites.

items.erreur_markdown: Using a frequency in MHz directly in $\lambda=c/f$ with $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, for example $\lambda=3.00\times10^{8}/98=3.06\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The speed is in metres per second, so the frequency must be in hertz: $98.0\ \mathrm{MHz}=9.80\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A VHF radio station broadcasts at $98.0\ \mathrm{MHz}$ and a UHF television station broadcasts at $600\ \mathrm{MHz}$. (a) Find the wavelength of each. (b) Find the energy of one photon of each and say which signal has the larger photon energy. ($c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\lambda=\dfrac{c}{f}$:

VHF: $\lambda=\dfrac{3.00\times10^{8}}{9.80\times10^{7}}=\mathbf{3.06\ m}$.

UHF: $\lambda=\dfrac{3.00\times10^{8}}{6.00\times10^{8}}=\mathbf{0.500\ m}$.

(b) $E=hf$:

VHF: $E=6.63\times10^{-34}\times9.80\times10^{7}=\mathbf{6.50\times10^{-26}\ J}$.

UHF: $E=6.63\times10^{-34}\times6.00\times10^{8}=\mathbf{3.98\times10^{-25}\ J}$.

The UHF photon has the larger energy, 6.12 times that of the VHF photon, because its frequency is higher.

items.enonce_markdown: A transmitter has a carrier frequency of $810\ \mathrm{kHz}$ and sends speech and music whose highest frequency is $5.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$ using amplitude modulation. (a) State the range of frequencies occupied and the bandwidth. (b) Which frequencies are present if the transmitter is modulated by a single pure tone of $3.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$? (c) How many such AM stations can share the band from $600\ \mathrm{kHz}$ to $700\ \mathrm{kHz}$ without overlapping? (d) How many FM stations, each needing $200\ \mathrm{kHz}$, fit into the band from $88\ \mathrm{MHz}$ to $108\ \mathrm{MHz}$?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The range is $f_c\pm f_m$, that is $810-5.0=805\ \mathrm{kHz}$ to $810+5.0=815\ \mathrm{kHz}$. The bandwidth is $2f_m=2\times5.0=\mathbf{10\ kHz}$.

(b) The frequencies are $f_c-f_m=\mathbf{807\ kHz}$, $f_c=\mathbf{810\ kHz}$ and $f_c+f_m=\mathbf{813\ kHz}$.

(c) The band is $700-600=100\ \mathrm{kHz}$ wide and each station needs $10\ \mathrm{kHz}$, so $\dfrac{100}{10}=\mathbf{10}$ stations.

(d) The band is $108-88=20\ \mathrm{MHz}=20\,000\ \mathrm{kHz}$ wide, so $\dfrac{20\,000}{200}=\mathbf{100}$ stations. FM can be used here because VHF has far more spectrum available than the medium-frequency band.

items.enonce_markdown: The tuned circuit of a radio receiver has a coil of inductance $150\ \mu\mathrm{H}$ and a variable capacitor whose capacitance can be set between $40\ \mathrm{pF}$ and $400\ \mathrm{pF}$. (a) Calculate the highest and the lowest frequency to which the circuit can be tuned. (b) Find the capacitance needed to receive a station of frequency $1.00\ \mathrm{MHz}$. (c) Show that a station of frequency $0.600\ \mathrm{MHz}$ cannot be received, and state one change which would allow it to be received.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$. The highest frequency uses the smallest capacitance:
$$f_{\max}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{150\times10^{-6}\times40\times10^{-12}}}=\mathbf{2.05\ MHz}$$
The lowest frequency uses the largest capacitance:
$$f_{\min}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{150\times10^{-6}\times400\times10^{-12}}}=\mathbf{0.650\ MHz}$$

(b) $C=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2L}=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi\times1.00\times10^{6})^2\times150\times10^{-6}}=\mathbf{169\ pF}$, which is inside the range $40$ to $400\ \mathrm{pF}$.

(c) For $0.600\ \mathrm{MHz}$ the same calculation gives $C=\mathbf{469\ pF}$, which is larger than $400\ \mathrm{pF}$, so the station is below the lowest frequency of the circuit ($0.650\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and cannot be tuned. Reception would be possible by increasing the inductance of the coil (or adding capacitance in parallel), because $f_0$ decreases when $L$ or $C$ increases.

items_markdown: A signal is a varying voltage, current or wave that carries information; modulation places it on a high-frequency carrier so that it can be radiated and different stations can share the spectrum.

VHF is very high frequency ($30$ to $300\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and UHF is ultra high frequency ($300\ \mathrm{MHz}$ to $3\ \mathrm{GHz}$); both travel as line-of-sight space waves and $E=hf$ gives a UHF photon more energy than a VHF photon.
In a receiver the LC loop selects the station by resonance, $f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, and the demodulator recovers the audio signal from the carrier.
AM varies the amplitude (narrow bandwidth, long range, more noise); FM varies the frequency (wide bandwidth, shorter range, less noise).

Cell phones use cells with base stations and reused frequencies; reception is poor behind concrete buildings because of absorption, shadow and multipath interference; roaming means using another operator's network away from the home network.
